Before We Start · A Tool You'll Use All Session

Reading a Lesion Backward

Willard opens every vascular session the same way, with a plain neuron and an axon, because the whole game of localizing a stroke is just this trick applied over and over.

Picture a neuron. It has a cell body and an axon, and that axon makes a synapse onto the next neuron down the line. Now cut the axon. Two separate things happen, in two separate places, and they are not the same event:

Baseline — an intact neuron, axon, and synapse.

Cut the axon (red mark) and the clock starts on both sides of the cut.

Cell body swells (chromatolysis). Everything distal to the cut wastes away (Wallerian degeneration).

🧠

Chromatolysis

What happens to the cell body that owns the cut axon. The nucleus pushes to the periphery, Nissl substance disperses, the soma swells. This is the neuron trying (and often failing) to repair itself.

✂️

Wallerian Degeneration

What happens to the axon distal to the cut — the part that's now disconnected from the cell body that was keeping it alive. It simply wastes away, all the way down to wherever it was headed.

Now scale that up from one axon to an entire nucleus. If you destroy a nucleus outright, every axon arriving at that nucleus gets cut where it enters — so every neuron that projects into the dead nucleus becomes chromatolytic. And every axon leaving that nucleus is now an orphaned axon with no cell body behind it — so it Wallerian-degenerates, all the way to its target.

Q: You destroy the ventral posterior lateral nucleus (VPL) of the thalamus in an infarct. Where do you find chromatolytic cell bodies, and where do you find Wallerian degeneration?

Answer

Chromatolysis shows up in the two places that send axons into VPL: the dorsal column nuclei (gracilis/cuneatus), whose medial lemniscus axons terminate there, and the postcentral gyrus, whose reciprocal corticothalamic axons also terminate there. Wallerian degeneration shows up in the projection VPL was sending out — the thalamocortical axons running up to postcentral gyrus. Reciprocal connections mean the postcentral gyrus neurons actually show up on both sides of the ledger: chromatolytic in their cell bodies (their axon into VPL was cut) and the source of a Wallerian-degenerating tract nowhere, since VPL's projection into them is what died. The trick, every time: ask what projects into the dead structure (chromatolysis) and what the dead structure projects out to (Wallerian degeneration).

🔑 Why This Matters For Vasculature

Every syndrome in this file is really the same exercise: a vessel dies, a patch of tissue with it, and everything wired into or out of that patch shows a predictable, traceable signature. Once you know the territory, you can predict the deficit. Once you know the deficit, you can work backward to the territory. That's the whole exam.

The Big Picture

Four Vessels In, Three Territories Out

Four great vessels climb into the skull. By the time they're done splitting, everything supratentorial belongs to one of three arteries: ACA, MCA, or PCA.

Two internal carotids and two vertebrals go up. The carotids each split into an MCA and an ACA. The two vertebrals join into a single basilar artery, which splits into the two PCAs. That's the whole map. Four pipes in, six arteries serving the cerebrum.

Netter Plate 131 — the full vessel tree, aortic arch to cerebrum. Click to zoom the labels.

Netter Plate 133a — the Circle of Willis dissected out, inferior view.

Large Vessel vs. Small Vessel Disease

Neurologists split stroke mechanism into two families, and the split matters because it changes how you treat the patient.

🩸

Large Vessel Disease — Embolic

Something breaks off elsewhere in the circulation and lodges in a big vessel — ICA, MCA, ACA, PCA, basilar. Onset is sudden. This is the pattern for most cortical strokes, including everything in this file.

🧱

Small Vessel Disease — Thrombotic

Lipohyalinosis: the vessel wall itself thickens with fatty material and the smooth muscle around it expands, slowly choking the lumen off from the inside. Gradual onset. This is the pattern behind most brainstem lacunar strokes.

Where Do the Emboli Come From?

  • Artery-to-artery — plaque breaks off the carotid and travels up.
  • Heart-to-artery — a clot forms on the wall of the heart (atrial fibrillation, post-MI mural thrombus) and travels up.
  • Paradoxical embolism — a clot starts as a venous problem (classically a deep vein thrombosis in the leg) and should be filtered out by the lungs. It only reaches the brain if there's a right-to-left shunt letting it skip the pulmonary circulation — the classic culprit is a patent foramen ovale (PFO).
💡 ELI5 — Why Almost Every First Stroke Is MCA

Think of the internal carotid as a hallway. MCA continues nearly straight ahead off that hallway. ACA peels off at a sharp angle, close to 90°. An embolus tumbling up the carotid at speed is going to keep going straight into MCA almost every time — it takes real luck (or a very specific push) to make that hard turn into ACA.

Where Does the Next Embolus Land?
Willard's own numbers from the review session — not a formal citation, just the rule of thumb he teaches.
First Stroke
MCA
~95%
ACA
~5%
Second Stroke (after the first MCA hit raises resistance)
MCA
~60%
ACA
~40%
Once one MCA is occluded, resistance in that pathway goes up, and the next embolus is meaningfully more likely to get pushed into ACA instead. A patient's second stroke is a different bet than their first.

Reading The Scan

Mapping the Territories

In the emergency room, you get an axial CT and a patient with symptoms. You need a fast, reliable way to say "that's MCA" or "that's ACA" without a radiology atlas in your hand.

The Internal Capsule Landmark Trick

On a standard axial slice through the basal ganglia, find the anterior and posterior limbs of the internal capsule — the two pale, V-shaped bands flanking the thalamus and lentiform nucleus. Extend each limb outward as an imaginary line. Those two lines divide the slice into three wedges:

  • Anterior wedge (in front of the anterior limb) — ACA territory.
  • Middle wedge (between the two limbs) — MCA territory.
  • Posterior wedge (behind the posterior limb) — PCA territory.

A change in density or signal that falls inside one of these three wedges tells you the vessel immediately — before you've read a single symptom off the chart.

🏥 Why This Is An ER Skill, Not Just A Test Answer

PCA territory covers almost all of the thalamus. MCA covers most of the basal ganglia, with ACA claiming a small anterior sliver. Once you can eyeball the wedge, you can call the vessel on a scan before you've even finished reading the chief complaint.

Which Vessel Actually Gets Hit?

Dong-Eog Kim and colleagues mapped 1,160 large-artery infarcts on diffusion-weighted MRI and sorted every one of them by which vessel was occluded. The result is about as close as you'll get to ground truth on how common each territory's stroke really is.

Cerebral Infarcts by Territory
Kim et al., Scientific Reports 9:11708 (2019) — 1,160 large-artery infarct patients, by occluded vessel.
MCA
896 pts · 77%
PCA
193 pts · 17%
ACA
71 pts · 6%
MCA territory also happens to be the biggest piece of supratentorial real estate — roughly 54% of the parenchymal volume, against ~13% each for ACA and PCA — so its dominance here is partly geography and partly the straight-shot embolic mechanics from the Big Picture section above.

Kim et al.'s own voxelwise frequency maps — MCA in red, ACA in green, PCA in blue, brightness scaled to how often a stroke lands on that voxel.

The Workhorse Vessel

Middle Cerebral Artery

MCA is where most strokes happen, so it's worth understanding its geography before splitting it into syndromes.

MCA runs between the temporal and frontal lobes, wraps around inside the insula, rises up, and emerges around the margin of the lateral (Sylvian) fissure. The cortex right along that margin is called the operculum, and on the dominant hemisphere the periopercular cortex is your language cortex — which is why language deficits dominate the MCA syndromes below.

Past the insula, MCA splits into two divisions, and this split is the single most important branch point in the whole lecture:

⬆️

Upper Division

Climbs onto the convexity of the frontal and anterior parietal cortex — motor strip, premotor cortex, Broca's area territory.

⬇️

Lower Division

Wraps onto the temporal lobe and reaches back to the supramarginal and angular gyri — Wernicke's area territory.

A lateral hemisphere specimen — the sylvian fissure runs the length of the operculum. Broca's area sits at the front of this territory (upper division), Wernicke's at the back (lower division).

🔑 The One Rule That Organizes Everything Below

Upper division syndromes are frontal / motor / expressive. Lower division syndromes are temporal / sensory / receptive. Learn that split once and every symptom list below just falls into place instead of needing to be memorized separately.

Deep to the cortex, small perforating branches called the lenticulostriate arteries (one of them classically named Huebner's artery) dive straight up into the basal ganglia. They're thin, they come off at a sharp angle under high pressure, and they rupture more readily than they occlude — which is why the basal ganglia are a classic site for hemorrhagic stroke rather than ischemic. More on that after the two MCA divisions.

MCA · Upper Division

The Frontal, Motor, Expressive Syndrome

Upper division territory covers the frontal eye fields, the motor strip's face/arm representation, Broca's area, and Exner's area. Damage it and the deficits are almost all about output.

One slice from a live case series reviewed in session — scroll through enough of these and the gray-white boundary loss becomes obvious.

🏥 A Practical ER Pearl

A fresh MCA occlusion can look like a completely normal CT in the first 24 hours — the density change hasn't caught up to the symptoms yet. One thing to look for: a faint white dot or line deep in the sylvian fissure, near the temporal lobe. That's the plugged MCA vessel itself, visible before the tissue damage is.

Dominant Side

Dominant Hemisphere
CategoryFinding
Cranial NervesLateral gaze palsy — eyes deviate toward the side of the lesion (frontal eye fields sit on the ACA/MCA watershed)
MotorSpastic facial palsy (central type) + weakness, Face > Arm > Leg
SensorySame gradient — Face > Arm > Leg
Mental StatusBroca's aphasia — low word output, effortful, broken speech, comprehension intact
Mental StatusAgraphia (damage to Exner's area, sitting just above Broca's)
Mental StatusApraxia — can't perform a movement to verbal command despite full strength
💡 ELI5 — Broca's Aphasia

The classic first patient described with this syndrome, a French farmer, could only say one syllable: "tan." That's the caricature of Broca's — low volume of words, and the words that do come out are broken and effortful. Comprehension is intact, which is exactly why these patients get frustrated with themselves: they know what they want to say and simply cannot get it out. That frustration-direction is your bedside test for distinguishing Broca's from a posterior aphasia.

⚠️ Two Different Kinds of Agraphia — Don't Merge Them

Exner's area agraphia (upper division, sits right above Broca's) is a graphomotor problem — the motor program for forming letters is damaged. Gerstmann's syndrome agraphia (lower division, angular gyrus — see below) is a linguistic problem. Same symptom name, two different mechanisms, two different territories.

🩺 On Apraxia

If you damage the premotor and motor cortex controlling someone's right hand and ask them to wave with the left hand, they may not be able to do it — despite full strength in that arm. Ask for an emotional wave (say goodbye to someone they love) and they may manage it fine. That gap between what a limb can do spontaneously and what it can do to verbal command is apraxia, and it's easy to miss on a quick exam. It becomes hugely important in rehab, where the question isn't "can this arm move" but "can this patient follow a work instruction with it."

Non-Dominant Side

Non-Dominant Hemisphere
CategoryFinding
Cranial NervesSame lateral gaze palsy
MotorSame facial palsy, Face > Arm > Leg
SensorySame gradient — Face > Arm > Leg
Mental StatusAprosodia — loses the sing-song melody of speech
Mental StatusAnosognosia — loss of awareness of the injury itself
🏥 Prosody Is Not A Minor Loss

A grade-school teacher known for controlling a rowdy classroom suffered a non-dominant stroke and lost her prosody. When she tried to return to teaching, she couldn't put emotional weight into her voice to say "quiet down" — the words were right, the melody that makes them land was gone. A huge amount of communication rides on how something is said, not just what is said.

The Homunculus Splits Two Ways
MCA territory is lateral, so it grabs the lateral homunculus (face, hand). ACA territory is medial, so it grabs the medial homunculus (leg). Schematic severity, not measured data.
MCA Upper Division (lateral motor strip)
Face

This is why an ACA-territory patient can swing a leg forward from the hip with real spasticity while their face and grip look almost normal — and why an MCA-upper patient's face droops hardest while their leg walks them out of the hospital.

Q: A patient has a left-sided lesion. Which way are their eyes deviated?

Answer

Toward the left — toward the lesion. Rule of thumb: with a destructive frontal eye field lesion, "you look at your lesion." (The frontal eye fields drive gaze to the opposite side; take one out and the unopposed healthy side wins, pushing the eyes toward the damaged side.)

MCA · Lower Division

The Temporal, Sensory, Receptive Syndrome

Lower division territory is temporal lobe and the posterior language cortex — Wernicke's area, the angular and supramarginal gyri, Meyer's loop. Motor strip and postcentral gyrus are largely untouched, so the deficits here are almost all about input and interpretation, not output.

A left lower-division MCA infarct — the wedge of hypodensity sits in temporal-parietal cortex, well away from the motor strip.

A higher slice, same patient — the same wedge tracking back toward the angular/supramarginal region.

Dominant Side

Dominant Hemisphere
CategoryFinding
Cranial NervesSuperior quadrantanopia ("pie in the sky") — Meyer's loop of the optic radiation swings out through the temporal lobe and runs straight through this territory
MotorGenerally spared — the lesion doesn't reach precentral gyrus
SensoryGenerally spared, for the same reason
Mental StatusWernicke's aphasia — fluent but empty speech, comprehension poor
Mental StatusGerstmann syndrome (angular gyrus) — see the four-part breakdown below
💡 ELI5 — Wernicke's vs. Broca's, the Fast Bedside Test

Ask who the patient is frustrated with. Broca's patients know exactly what they want to say and get frustrated with themselves for not being able to produce it. Wernicke's patients produce fluent, grammatical-sounding speech that doesn't actually make sense, don't fully realize it, and get frustrated with you for not understanding them.

🩺 A Case: The Riding Instructor

A woman who taught horseback riding suffered a lower-division MCA stroke that tracked all the way back into occipital cortex on imaging. Her motor exam was essentially normal — she went back to riding. What she couldn't do was teach again: a profound Wernicke's aphasia with comprehension badly affected. Worth noting: women tend to have a larger splenium of the corpus callosum, which gives some bilateral back-up for language and makes Wernicke's-type aphasia somewhat less devastating on average than in men with an equivalent lesion.

🔑 Gerstmann Syndrome — The Angular Gyrus Tetrad

Four findings, one small patch of dominant parietal cortex:

  • Acalculia — can't do math
  • Finger agnosia — can't tell their own index from middle from ring finger
  • Agraphia — a linguistic writing deficit (contrast with Exner's agraphia, upper division)
  • Left-right disorientation

Non-Dominant Side

Non-Dominant Hemisphere
CategoryFinding
Cranial NervesSame superior quadrantanopia pattern possible
Motor / SensoryGenerally spared
Mental StatusAsomatognosia — loss of body ownership; the limb feels like it isn't theirs
Mental StatusNeglect (can be mild, and mild neglect is the dangerous kind — see below)
🩺 A Case: "The Damn Thing Has Me"

A woman in a wheelchair, well after a profound non-dominant stroke, was asked if she had a left hand. "Of course I have a left hand," she said, and showed it. Asked if she could walk, she said yes — asked to show it, she said "well, I can't, because the damn thing has me," referring to her own left arm, hooked in the wheelchair strap. She acknowledged something was there. She simply wouldn't claim it as hers. That's asomatognosia layered with a loss of self-awareness — two related but separable deficits that often travel together.

⚠️ Why Mild Neglect Is the Dangerous Kind

By definition, a patient who is neglecting one side doesn't know they're doing it — and neither does anyone around them, if the neglect is subtle. Two quick bedside tests: extinction testing (touch both sides simultaneously with equal, loud stimuli — a neglecting patient reports only the dominant side, even though they correctly identify either side alone) and line bisection (ask the patient to mark the center of a horizontal line — how far their mark drifts from true center is a rough index of how much they're neglecting). An elderly driver who's had three minor accidents on the left side of the car in one week just failed an informal version of this test.

Q: A patient can produce fluent, grammatical speech, but none of it makes sense, and their comprehension is poor. Broca's or Wernicke's — and which division of MCA?

Answer

Wernicke's aphasia, dominant lower division MCA.

Aside — Bedside Cognitive Screening

When temporal lobe damage raises concern for a broader memory problem, a quick Mini-Mental / Folstein-style screen is the move: serial 7s, spelling a word backward, three-object recall at five minutes, and copying two intersecting pentagons.

A real patient attempt at the intersecting-pentagons task — the shapes don't overlap correctly, a classic visuospatial red flag.

When MCA Bleeds Instead of Clogs

The Lenticulostriate Hemorrhage

Not every basal ganglia catastrophe is ischemic. The same small perforating vessels that feed the deep structures are also the ones most likely to burst.

The lenticulostriate arteries (Huebner's artery among them) are thin, take off from MCA and ACA at sharp angles, and run under high pressure straight into the striatum. That combination — thin wall, sharp angle, high pressure — makes them prone to rupture rather than occlusion. When one bursts, blood dissects straight into the basal ganglia.

Coronal gross specimen — a fresh hemorrhage occupying the basal ganglia, exactly where the lenticulostriate perforators dive in.

Gross specimen, coronal section — a large intraparenchymal hemorrhage occupying the deep white matter, the pathology behind the bright-white finding you'd see acutely on CT.

🏥 The Practical Takeaway

MCA does a huge amount of cortex, but it also has this deep component supplying the anterior basal ganglia — and that deep component is your classic source of a hypertensive basal ganglia bleed. On CT, that's the difference between chasing a dark wedge (ischemia) and a bright clot (hemorrhage), and it changes the entire acute management pathway.

The Medial Vessel

Anterior Cerebral Artery

ACA takes the medial surface of the hemisphere — cingulate gyrus, medial frontal cortex, the medial sliver of motor/sensory strip. Smaller territory, sharply different symptom set from MCA.

Past the anterior communicating artery, ACA divides into the pericallosal artery (runs right along the corpus callosum) and the callosomarginal artery (runs along the outside of the cingulate gyrus). Deep medial striate branches reach into the medial basal ganglia — but notably, they don't reach the thalamus (that's PCA territory).

The medial surface, labeled — the paracentral lobule (leg motor/sensory) and cingulate gyrus sit squarely in ACA territory; cuneus/lingual gyrus (visual cortex, bottom) belong to PCA — keep this picture in mind for both sections.

⚠️ The ACA-ACA "Steal" — Why One Rupture Can Cause a Bilateral Stroke

The two ACAs are connected by the anterior communicating artery, which means if one side goes down, the other side can supply across the midline and rescue it — useful collateral, right up until it isn't. If one ACA hemorrhages, the healthy side can get "stolen from" trying to compensate, and you can end up with a second, ischemic infarct on the originally-healthy side. One rupture, two strokes, both ACA territories, both legs.

🩺 A Case: The Ruptured ACA Aneurysm

A man was found unresponsive, face-down, after being alone for over a day. Imaging showed the classic "star sign" — blood filling the basal cisterns in a radiating pattern — plus blood tracking into the frontal lobe, then breaking through into the lateral, third, and fourth ventricles. The source: a saccular aneurysm off ACA. Blood in the ventricular system is an ominous sign, but he survived, and the aneurysm was treated by threading a coil into the sac — the coil clots off, then fibroses, sealing the aneurysm from the inside.

The "star sign" — blood in the basal cisterns radiating outward, with the starburst artifact of a coil already in place.

Blood filling the lateral ventricles — bright white tracking through the foramen of Monro.

Catheter angiogram, same mechanism — the coiled aneurysm sac is visible as a dense round tangle.

A different patient, days later — low density on both sides after the "steal" phenomenon converted a unilateral rupture into a bilateral infarct.

The ACA Syndrome

CategoryDominant SideNon-Dominant Side
Cranial NervesGaze palsy possible (frontal eye fields sit on the ACA/MCA watershed)Same
MotorLeg > Arm > Face — the opposite gradient from MCA upper divisionSame
SensoryLeg > Arm > FaceSame

💡 ELI5 — Why Legs, Not Faces

The motor and sensory homunculus is folded over the top of the brain like a strip running from lateral (face, hand) to medial (trunk, leg). MCA owns the lateral surface, so it grabs face and hand hardest. ACA owns the medial surface, so it grabs the leg hardest and barely touches the face. Same strip of cortex, opposite ends, opposite vessel.

🩺 A Case: The Classic ACA Presentation

A young man, after a weekend of heavy cocaine use, hemorrhaged and ended up wheelchair-bound. Both legs were intensely spastic — he couldn't stand or walk on them. His hands, though clumsy with some spasticity, still worked well enough to move things and could have operated a motorized wheelchair. His face was essentially unaffected. Leg > arm > face, textbook ACA.

The Apathy → Abulia → Akinetic Mutism Spectrum

ACA territory connects into the anterior/midline thalamic nuclei, which is why this syndrome bleeds into emotion, memory, and motivation — not just movement. Motivational loss runs along a continuum:

  1. Apathy — the patient is calm, present, and willing to let a spouse answer every question for them. Not because they can't participate, but because they don't feel driven to.
  2. Abulia — motivation drops further. The patient will respond to a physical stimulus like a pinch, acknowledging it, but won't meaningfully engage verbally.
  3. Akinetic mutism — the patient can look completely unresponsive, almost catatonic. This is not unconsciousness. They may still be taking in everything said around them, which means bedside conversation should be conducted as if they're listening — because they may well be. A useful first check: lift the eyes and tip the head back and watch whether the eyes track, which confirms the brainstem (and likely more) is still engaged.
🏥 What Patients Say Afterward

Patients who recover from akinetic mutism sometimes describe the experience simply as "I didn't feel like I had anything to say." They were aware. They lacked the drive to respond — which is the whole point of calling this a motivation spectrum rather than a consciousness spectrum.

🔑 Two Separate Causes of Incontinence Here

The medial motor strip has a direct representation for bladder control (roughly S2–4). Damage that, and the patient loses bladder control outright — more reliably with bilateral lesions than unilateral. Just in front of that sits a separate premotor region that coordinates social timing of voiding, and further forward still, a prefrontal region that holds the social rules around when it's appropriate to void. Damage only the social-rules region (as seen in frontotemporal dementia and Alzheimer's) and the patient keeps physical bladder control but loses the social judgment about when to use it.

Q: A patient has a language deficit after an ACA stroke, but unlike a typical Broca's aphasia, they can repeat a phrase you give them even though they can't generate speech spontaneously. What is this, and why does it differ from Broca's?

Answer

Transcortical motor aphasia. The lesion here spares the perisylvian language loop itself (including the arcuate fasciculus that supports repetition) and instead disconnects the supplementary/medial frontal region that drives spontaneous speech initiation. Prompting and repetition work; self-generated language doesn't. A large enough ACA lesion reaching further back can produce a mixed transcortical aphasia, with both poor comprehension and poor spontaneous output.

The Back Of The House

Posterior Cerebral Artery

PCA territory is thalamus plus the entire occipital lobe plus the medial and inferior temporal lobe. Motor strip is untouched, so — like MCA's lower division — this syndrome is dominated by vision, memory, and language comprehension rather than movement.

PCA runs forward along the medial temporal lobe almost to its tip, then fans out to claim nearly all of visual cortex. MCA approaches the same territory from the lateral side, which sets up an important overlap zone right at the very center of the visual field.

Inferior temporal-occipital surface, labeled — fusiform, parahippocampal, and lingual gyri, the territory behind the naming and object-recognition deficits below.

💡 ELI5 — Macular Sparing

The very center of your visual field — the fovea — has its cortical representation sitting right on the watershed between MCA and PCA, so it effectively gets blood from both. Knock out PCA and the peripheral visual field goes dark, but that small central island often survives on MCA's contribution alone. That preserved central island, in an otherwise blind hemifield, is called macular sparing, and it's a reliable PCA signature.

CategoryDominant SideNon-Dominant Side
Cranial NervesHomonymous hemianopia with macular sparingSame
Motor / SensoryGenerally sparedGenerally spared
Mental StatusMemory loss, more verbal/linguistic in characterMemory loss, more spatial in character
Mental StatusAnomia and/or agnosia (see distinction below)Neglect can occur, usually milder than lower-division MCA
Mental StatusTranscortical sensory aphasia — fluent, poor comprehension, benefits from prompting—
PerceptualVisual and/or olfactory hallucinationsSame, plus rare prosopagnosia (face blindness)

Gross specimen, medial surface — the darkened, congested tissue at the occipital pole marks a PCA territory infarct.

A PCA territory infarct on CT, different patient.

Anomia vs. Agnosia — Not the Same Deficit

Both live in this territory, but they're functionally distinct, and the distinction shows up cleanly at the bedside:

🏷️

Anomia

Damage nearer the temporal pole (naming/memory-of-names territory). The patient knows exactly what an object is and how to use it — they simply cannot retrieve its name.

❓

Agnosia

Damage further back, nearer visual cortex. The patient can't identify what the object is or how it's used at all — a deeper failure of recognition, not just retrieval.

🩺 A Case: "Car Starter Things"

A man with a long history of alcohol use and repeated forward falls (significant temporal lobe trauma) was handed a set of keys and asked what they were. "Everyone has them," he said. Pressed for the actual name, he called them "car starter things." He clearly knew what they did — he just couldn't retrieve the word "keys." That's anomia without agnosia: the object-knowledge is intact, the label is gone.

🏥 Prosopagnosia

Rare, but worth knowing: patients lose the ability to recognize faces — even a spouse's — by sight alone. They can still recognize the person the moment that person speaks, since voice recognition runs through a different pathway entirely. All faces start to look interchangeable to them.

Why Visual and Olfactory Hallucinations Travel Together

Primary olfactory cortex sits over the uncus, and secondary olfactory cortex sits just behind it on the parahippocampal gyrus — right next door to the occipitotemporal visual association cortex. Damage in this neighborhood can trigger hallucinations in either modality, which is exactly why this region is also the classic origin point for temporal lobe (focal) seizures: an aura that often starts as a foul, unpleasant smell that isn't actually there.

⚠️ Why the Hippocampus Is So Fragile

The pyramidal cell layer of the hippocampus fires at very high frequency — that's the oscillating loop that helps engrain a memory onto cortex in the first place. The tradeoff for that high-frequency firing is extreme sensitivity to anoxia (a few minutes of poor oxygenation can wipe out the CA1 layer specifically, producing a profound anterograde amnesia) and a tendency to misfire into seizure once inhibition drops even slightly.

A Different Kind of PCA Problem: Compression, Not Occlusion

PCA doesn't just get occluded — it can be physically compressed. The vessel wraps directly around the crus cerebri, right where the crus sits against the tentorial incisura (the sharp free edge of the tentorium cerebelli). A mass effect that shifts the brain against that edge can pinch both the trochlear nerve and PCA at the same spot.

🩺 A Case: The Snowboarder

A woman fell while snowboarding, struck her head, and initially had a relatively unremarkable neuro exam — until a large visual field cut showed up on follow-up imaging that wasn't there on her initial workup. As swelling progressed, her brain shifted against the tentorial incisura, and the sharp edge compressed the opposite cerebral peduncle against the tentorium. The result was a striking, counterintuitive combination: a right-sided head injury producing right-sided spasticity (from compression of the left peduncle) plus a homonymous hemianopia (from PCA compression at the same location). This is a false localizing sign — the spasticity side doesn't point to the side of the original injury, it points to which peduncle got pinched.

Alexia Without Agraphia

This one came up as a question mid-session, and it's worth walking through slowly because it only makes sense once you trace the whole circuit.

  1. Normal reading, step by step: visual cortex on either side registers the printed word. On the dominant side it's a short hop to Wernicke's area for translation into language. On the non-dominant side, the visual information has to cross the midline through the splenium of the corpus callosum before it can reach the dominant Wernicke's area.
  2. Now destroy dominant visual cortex plus the splenium (a rare but very instructive lesion pattern — classically a PCA territory infarct that also nicks the splenium). The patient can still see out of their intact non-dominant visual cortex.
  3. They can still write — the motor/language circuitry for producing language (including Exner's area) is untouched and doesn't depend on this pathway.
  4. But they cannot read what they just wrote. The visual information from their intact non-dominant cortex has nowhere to go: dominant visual cortex is dead, and the splenium that would have routed it across to Wernicke's is also gone. They can see the letters. They cannot translate them into language.
🔑 The Net Result: Alexia Without Agraphia

Writing survives. Reading — even reading their own handwriting, moments after writing it — does not. It's a strange, specific, and genuinely rare disconnection syndrome, and it only makes sense once you've traced the visual-to-Wernicke's pathway on both sides of the brain.

The Border Zone

The Watershed Territory

Every place two territories meet, there's a strip of cortex living at the very end of both blood supplies — well fed by either vessel alone, but the first tissue to suffer when perfusion pressure drops globally rather than from a single blocked vessel.

The watershed band, lateral and medial views — the border strip between ACA/MCA (and, further back, MCA/PCA).

💡 ELI5 — Two Very Different Ways to Lose a Watershed Function

Take the frontal eye fields — they sit right on the ACA/MCA watershed. Knock out one of those two vessels and the eye fields typically go down from swelling but come back over the following days, because the other vessel was covering that patch of cortex the whole time. That's the upside of straddling a watershed. The downside shows up when both vessels drop together — a global perfusion problem, not a single clogged pipe — and now the one strip of cortex that depended on both is the one strip that gets no rescue. That's a true watershed infarct.

The Adult Watershed Infarct

A true watershed infarct comes from a drop in global perfusion pressure — profound hypotension, cardiac arrest, a severe bleed — not from a single vessel occlusion. Because the entire border zone is starved at once, the infarct traces the border zone itself: a curved, almost C-shaped band running between ACA and MCA territory. That band crosses the motor strip right around the trunk and hip representation — which is why a watershed stroke has a very particular motor signature.

FLAIR sequence, bilateral watershed injury in a patient with a prolonged hypotensive episode.

Bilateral, fairly symmetric change in the centrum semiovale — the internal (subcortical) watershed.

DWI — acute injury lights up bright on diffusion, tracing the watershed band.

T2WI, same patient — the anatomical counterpart, less conspicuous than the DWI.

🔑 Cortical Watershed vs. Internal Watershed

There are actually two watershed zones, not one. The well-known one is cortical — the ACA/MCA/PCA border on the brain's surface. The less-publicized one is internal (subcortical) — the border between superficial pial-plexus perforators and the deep penetrating branches off the basal cerebral arteries, running through the white matter of the corona radiata and centrum semiovale. When the internal watershed infarct is confluent (a solid stripe rather than scattered dots), outcomes are meaningfully worse.

Superficial pial-plexus branches and deep penetrating branches, numbered and traced separately — the internal watershed is the border zone between these two systems.

🩺 A Case: The Crashing Blood Pressure

A patient in crisis was running a blood pressure well over 200 systolic — the result, though nobody recognized it in the moment, of a surge of catecholamines the body was pumping out. EMS did exactly what you'd normally want for a hypertensive emergency: they gave medication to bring the pressure down. But once the catecholamine surge burned itself out, the blood pressure didn't just normalize — it kept falling, plummeting well past a safe floor. That crash in perfusion pressure, arriving right on the heels of the treatment, produced a watershed infarct. It's a reminder that treating the number in front of you without understanding the mechanism behind it can create a second emergency.

The Neonatal Watershed: Two Very Different Babies

The same border-zone logic applies at birth — but where the watershed physically sits, and what it does to a baby, depends entirely on how mature that baby's brain is when the perfusion drop happens.

👶

Term Neonate → Parasagittal Injury

In a full-term baby, the watershed sits at the vertex — the same cortical border zone as an adult. A perfusion drop during a difficult birth (cord compression, early placental separation) produces a wedge-shaped injury crossing the motor strip at the trunk/proximal-limb level. The result is a spastic pattern, heaviest around the shoulders and hips.

🍼

Preterm Neonate (26–34 wks) → Periventricular Leukomalacia

In a premature brain, the watershed hasn't matured outward yet — it sits close to the ventricles instead. The same kind of perfusion insult now damages periventricular white matter. For reasons that aren't fully worked out, the resulting weakness is flaccid rather than spastic, and it's concentrated in the lower extremities.

Parasagittal injury — term neonate. The injury band sits at the vertex, hitting the proximal (shoulder/hip) motor representation hardest.

Periventricular leukomalacia — preterm neonate. The injury band sits near the ventricles, hitting the lower-extremity white matter hardest.

🏥 Both Get Labeled "Cerebral Palsy" — But They Look Different At The Bedside

A term baby with parasagittal injury develops elevated extensor tone and classically walks up onto their toes, heels never quite reaching the ground — and instead of a normal crawl, the legs kick out stiffly behind them while the arms do the work. A preterm baby with periventricular leukomalacia instead develops a flaccid, lower-extremity-predominant weakness. Same eventual diagnosis category, two distinguishable mechanisms, two distinguishable exams.

Q (from the slide deck): In parasagittal injury, the clinical findings are focused on the — head/neck, shoulder/arm, forearm/wrist/hand, low back/thigh, or leg/ankle/foot?

Answer

Shoulder and arm (paired with hip/thigh on the opposite end of the same proximal-predominant pattern) — the watershed at the vertex hits the proximal limb representation hardest, not the distal hand/foot or the head/neck.

Q (from the slide deck): In periventricular leukomalacia, the clinical findings are focused on the — head/neck, shoulder/arm, forearm/wrist/hand, low back/thigh, or leg/ankle/foot?

Answer

Leg, ankle, and foot — the medially-shifted periventricular watershed in a premature brain lands squarely on the lower-extremity white matter.

🔑 The One-Line Summary For This Whole Section

Same mechanism — a border zone starved by a global perfusion drop, not a single occluded vessel — but the border zone moves depending on how mature the brain is (adult and term-neonate: vertex/cortical; preterm neonate: periventricular), and where it lands determines everything about the resulting exam.
